title: Hypokalaemia
clinicalScenario: Outline only. Planned scope: Severity by level and ECG, oral versus intravenous replacement and rate limits, magnesium, causes, monitoring. Candidate sources to verify: NHS trust potassium replacement protocols; US ED references to be confirmed.

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult (over 18 years) Emergency Department (ED) recognition and replacement of hypokalaemia, based on the NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service (SPS) hypokalaemia article and a Scottish emergency medicine guideline "Emergency Management of Hypokalaemia in Adults". No Saudi national hypokalaemia guideline was found; this protocol adopts the SPS and Scottish recommendations as the Saudi reference. Paediatric care and long-term management are outside this protocol.
findings: Full protocol rebuilt from the source dossier opened on 2026-10-21; exact source locations are recorded in each investigation and medicine row.
The original outline remains preserved; this additive version is non-current and pending clinical review.
unverifiedSections: Normal reference ranges are typical adult values, not taken from the cited sources; ranges differ between laboratories.
Symptoms, signs, precipitants, differentials and pathophysiology are standard clinical content and were not extracted line by line from the sources.

Neither source is paginated, so section headings are cited; the Scottish guideline does not state its issuing organisation or date, so it should be replaced with a dated guideline before clinical sign-off.
The Scottish guideline lists 10 and 20 mmol/hour without making clear which indication each rate applies to; the maximum rate here follows NHS SPS.

The Gloucestershire and Worcestershire guidelines were past their stated review date (March 2026); check for newer versions. Their oral doses differ by level (for example moderate: 96 versus 72 mmol/day); both are shown, each with its own level band. Sando-K is 12 mmol potassium per tablet and Kay-Cee-L is 1 mmol/mL: these were derived from the quoted daily totals and must be checked against the product label. Bag duration (40 mmol over 4 hours at 10 mmol/hour) is arithmetic, not quoted. The 20–40 mmol/L initial IV figure for mild disease is ambiguous in the source.

No Saudi national or Saudi Ministry of Health hypokalaemia guideline was found; Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) registration and availability of ready-mixed potassium chloride and magnesium sulphate were not checked.
The oral potassium doses do not give a maximum duration or total daily maximum; hospital pharmacy limits apply.

Renal, hepatic and age adjustments for the drugs added in this revision are from manufacturer labels (UK Summary of Product Characteristics, US prescribing information and a New Zealand data sheet), not from Saudi Food and Drug Authority labels.

pathophysiology.summary: Hypokalaemia is a serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L.
keyMechanisms: Potassium is lost through the gut (vomiting, diarrhoea) or kidneys (diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, magnesium depletion).
Potassium moves into cells with insulin, beta-agonists and alkalosis.
Low extracellular potassium delays repolarisation, producing U waves, T-wave flattening, ST changes and arrhythmias, most often ventricular tachycardia.
Magnesium depletion makes hypokalaemia resistant to replacement.

symptoms: Weakness, lethargy, constipation and palpitations in moderate disease.
redFlags: Potassium below 2.5 mmol/L (severe), with muscle necrosis and arrhythmias.
precipitants: Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, insulin treatment (for example diabetic ketoacidosis), magnesium depletion, poor intake, beta-agonists.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Episodic paralysis with normal potassium between attacks
Low magnesium; hypokalaemia that does not correct
Hypertension with low potassium and metabolic alkalosis
Delayed sample with very high white cell count

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Grade severity and choose oral or IV replacement; target 4.0–4.5 mmol/L

references.title: Emergency Management of Hypokalaemia in Adults
references.edition: Scottish emergency medicine guideline (website cem.scot.nhs.uk), organisation and date not stated; section Life-threatening hypokalaemia

clinicalManagement.title: Immediate
actions: Get an urgent ECG and check potassium and magnesium.
Cardiac arrest: start Advanced Life Support, treat hypokalaemia and give magnesium sulphate 10 mmol IV while awaiting the magnesium level.
Life-threatening hypokalaemia: give IV potassium chloride with monitoring and seek expert help.
IV potassium must be given in a hospital with appropriate monitoring.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing
actions: Preparation: use a ready-mixed premixed bag only (potassium chloride 0.3% = 40 mmol in 1 L 0.9% sodium chloride, or 0.15% = 20 mmol in 1 L). Never add potassium to a bag on the ward and never put magnesium and potassium in the same bag. Use an infusion pump.
Recheck potassium after every 40 mmol of potassium chloride with normal renal function, or every 20 mmol with severe renal impairment.
Aim for a potassium of 4.0–4.5 mmol/L.
Replace magnesium if low; this allows faster correction of potassium.
Find and treat the cause, and stop or review potassium-losing medicines.

clinicalManagement.title: Escalation
actions: Arrhythmia or arrest: expert help immediately.
Rates above 20 mmol/hour need cardiac monitoring.

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition
actions: Admit for IV replacement, ECG changes or severe or symptomatic hypokalaemia.

regimens.genericName: Potassium effervescent tablets (Sando-K; 12 mmol potassium per tablet, derived from 2 tablets = 24 mmol)
regimens.dose: 2 tablets (24 mmol) per dose, dissolved in a glass of water, taken with or after food. Gloucestershire: 2 tablets three times daily (72 mmol/day). Worcestershire: 2 tablets twice daily (48 mmol/day)
regimens.frequency: Three times daily (Gloucestershire) or twice daily (Worcestershire)
regimens.duration: Until potassium is 3.5 mmol/L or above; check potassium daily
adjustments: contact the renal team if on dialysis or severe renal impairment
monitoring: U&E daily until normal, or on the documented review date
contraindications: stop if vomiting or abdominal distress and use IV

learningObjectives: Grade hypokalaemia and recognise ECG changes.
Choose oral or IV replacement safely, with correct concentration and rate.
pitfalls: Giving concentrated potassium by a peripheral line.
Giving too much potassium in renal impairment.
Forgetting to recheck potassium after every 40 mmol (20 mmol in severe renal impairment).
keyPoints: Check magnesium; potassium will not correct without it.
IV potassium needs monitoring and limited concentration.
